section_summary.extract_value: This Results section (no explicit study label) reports analyses on a single sample (N = 509). Missing data (<2%) were mean-replaced; Table 1 presents descriptive statistics and bivariate correlations where body appreciation was reported as significantly negatively correlated with BMI and Neuroticism and positively correlated with Extraversion and subjective social status. Hierarchical regressions predicting drive for muscularity and body appreciation included subjective social status, BMI and BMI^2, and Big Five domains; Neuroticism and BMI predicted drive for muscularity, while Neuroticism (strongest), subjective social status, BMI, and Extraversion predicted body appreciation. No 'Study 1'/'Experiment 2' labels or multiple sample subsets are mentioned.
section_summary.evidence_source: Missing data (<2%) were replaced using the mean replacement technique. Note. N = 509. Descriptive statistics for, and bivariate correlations between, all variables are reported in Table 1. On the other hand, body appreciation was significantly and negatively correlated with Neuroticism and BMI, and positively correlated with Extraversion and subjective social status. We next computed two separate hierarchical regressions with drive for muscularity and body appreciation, respectively, as the criterion variables. To examine for the possibility of curvilinear relationships with BMI, both BMI and BMI^2 were entered in a first step along with subjective social status. The Big Five domains were entered in a second step. Consistent with our hypothesis... the model with drive for muscularity was significant... with Neuroticism and participant BMI emerging as the only significant predictors. In the model with body appreciation... Neuroticism emerging as the strongest predictor. Subjective social status, BMI, and Extraversion also emerged as significant predictors.
